CALIFORNIA SOLAR RIGHTS ACT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield · Maple Grove Homeowners Association

CALIFORNIA SOLAR RIGHTS ACT — INTRODUCTION AND SCOPE
This information sheet describes, in general terms, the California Solar Rights Act provisions found at Civil Code § 714 and § 714.1, in connection with the property located at 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield and, where applicable, the common interest development association Maple Grove Homeowners Association. Civil Code § 714 makes void and unenforceable any covenant, restriction, or condition in a deed, contract, security instrument, or other transfer instrument, and any provision of a common interest development governing document, that effectively prohibits or restricts the installation or use of a solar energy system — subject to a statutory exception for restrictions that are genuinely "reasonable" as the statute defines that term. It covers the general voiding rule; the line the statute draws between a permissible reasonable restriction and a prohibited effective ban, including the different numeric cost and efficiency thresholds the statute sets for solar water-heating and pool-heating systems versus photovoltaic systems; the health, safety, and technical standards a solar energy system may still be required to meet; the timeline within which an association or other approving entity must act on an application, including the 45-day deemed-approved rule; the specific restrictions Civil Code § 714.1 permits (and forbids) a common interest development association to impose; and the damages, civil penalty, and attorney's-fee remedies the statute provides for a willful violation. This topic is distinct from a seller's document-disclosure obligations to a buyer under the Davis-Stirling Act (addressed in this corpus's HOA/CC&R Disclosure document) and from an association's assessment lien and foreclosure remedy for unpaid assessments (addressed in this corpus's HOA Assessment Lien and Foreclosure — Information Sheet). This sheet is informational only. It does not itself approve, deny, install, modify, or evaluate any solar energy system; it does not interpret, amend, or apply any specific deed, CC&R, or governing document affecting 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield; and it does not determine whether any actual covenant, restriction, condition, association action, or application-review decision relating to 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield or Maple Grove Homeowners Association complies — or fails to comply — with the statutory requirements it describes.

COVENANTS AND RESTRICTIONS THAT EFFECTIVELY PROHIBIT SOLAR ARE VOID
California's Solar Rights Act states a general rule voiding private restrictions on solar energy systems. Civil Code § 714(a) provides: "Any covenant, restriction, or condition contained in any deed, contract, security instrument, or other instrument affecting the transfer or sale of, or any interest in, real property, and any provision of a governing document, as defined in Section 4150 or 6552, that effectively prohibits or restricts the installation or use of a solar energy system is void and unenforceable." By its terms, this rule reaches restrictions in deeds, contracts, and security instruments affecting real property generally, and separately reaches any provision of a common interest development "governing document" (a term the statute cross-references to Civil Code § 4150 or § 6552). The statute's use of the phrase "effectively prohibits or restricts" means the voiding rule can reach a restriction that does not use the word "solar" or "prohibit" at all, if its practical effect is to prohibit or restrict solar installation or use. This general rule is qualified by a statutory exception for reasonable restrictions, addressed elsewhere in this corpus. This description concerns the statutory rule generally; it does not determine whether any specific covenant, restriction, or condition affecting 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield is void or unenforceable under it.

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 714(a) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 714(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=714.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes a single subdivision, Civil Code § 714(a); it is one source, not independently corroborated by a second source. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's Solar Rights Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property; other states impose different or no comparable solar-restriction voiding rule. This clause does not address the reasonable-restrictions exception referenced in § 714(a)'s companion subdivision (b), which is covered in a separate clause in this corpus, nor does it resolve what the cross-referenced governing-document definitions in Civil Code § 4150 or § 6552 provide, since those sections were not independently fetched or verified for this clause.

THE LINE BETWEEN A PERMISSIBLE "REASONABLE RESTRICTION" AND A PROHIBITED EFFECTIVE BAN
Civil Code § 714 does not void every restriction that touches a solar energy system — it carves out restrictions the statute itself defines as "reasonable." Section 714(b) provides: "This section does not apply to provisions that impose reasonable restrictions on solar energy systems. However, it is the policy of the state to promote and encourage the use of solar energy systems and to remove obstacles thereto. Accordingly, reasonable restrictions on a solar energy system are those restrictions that do not significantly increase the cost of the system or significantly decrease its efficiency or specified performance, or that allow for an alternative system of comparable cost, efficiency, and energy conservation benefits." The statute then gives "significantly" a precise, quantified meaning that differs by category of system. Section 714(d)(1)(A) provides that "[f]or solar domestic water heating systems or solar swimming pool heating systems that comply with state and federal law, ‘significantly’ means an amount exceeding 10 percent of the cost of the system, but in no case more than one thousand dollars ($1,000), or decreasing the efficiency of the solar energy system by an amount exceeding 10 percent, as originally specified and proposed." Section 714(d)(1)(B) sets a different formula for a different category of system: "For photovoltaic systems that comply with state and federal law, ‘significantly’ means an amount not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000) over the system cost as originally specified and proposed, or a decrease in system efficiency of an amount exceeding 10 percent as originally specified and proposed." In practical terms, for a solar water-heating or pool-heating system the statutory cost threshold is whichever is smaller of 10% of the system's cost or $1,000, while for a photovoltaic system the statutory cost threshold is a flat $1,000 over the originally specified and proposed cost; both categories share the same 10%-efficiency-decrease threshold. This description concerns the statutory reasonable-restriction standard generally; it does not calculate or determine whether any specific restriction, cost impact, or efficiency impact affecting 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield falls within or outside that standard.

The statute defines "significantly" only for cost and efficiency impacts; it does not, in the text quoted here, separately define a numeric threshold for the "specified performance" language used in § 714(b), and this clause does not speculate about what a performance-based (as opposed to cost- or efficiency-based) restriction would require. This clause also does not address § 714.1's separate, HOA-specific list of restrictions an association may or may not impose, which is covered in a different clause in this corpus.

HEALTH, SAFETY, AND TECHNICAL STANDARDS A SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEM MAY STILL BE REQUIRED TO MEET
Civil Code § 714's voiding rule does not exempt a solar energy system from otherwise-applicable health, safety, and technical standards. Section 714(c)(1) provides: "A solar energy system shall meet applicable health and safety standards and requirements imposed by state and local permitting authorities, consistent with Section 65850.5 of the Government Code." Two more specific technical requirements follow, again distinguishing solar water-heating systems from photovoltaic systems. Section 714(c)(2) provides: "Solar energy systems used for heating water in single family residences and solar collectors used for heating water in commercial or swimming pool applications shall be certified by an accredited listing agency as defined in the Plumbing and Mechanical Codes." Section 714(c)(3) provides: "A solar energy system for producing electricity shall also meet all applicable safety and performance standards established by the California Electrical Code, the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, and accredited testing laboratories such as Underwriters Laboratories and, where applicable, rules of the Public Utilities Commission regarding safety and reliability." These technical-compliance requirements exist independently of, and are not themselves voided by, the reasonable-restriction standard described elsewhere in this corpus. This description concerns the statutory technical-standards requirements generally; it does not determine whether any specific solar energy system proposed or installed at 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield meets them.

PROCESSING A SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEM APPLICATION: THE 45-DAY DEEMED-APPROVED RULE
Civil Code § 714 regulates not only the substance of solar restrictions but also the process an approving entity — including a homeowners association — must follow when a solar energy system application requires approval. Section 714(e)(1) provides: "Whenever approval is required for the installation or use of a solar energy system, the application for approval shall be processed and approved by the appropriate approving entity in the same manner as an application for approval of an architectural modification to the property, and shall not be willfully avoided or delayed." For an association that is not a public entity, the statute adds two further requirements and a firm deadline. Section 714(e)(2)(A) provides: "The approval or denial of an application shall be in writing." Section 714(e)(2)(B) provides: "If an application is not denied in writing within 45 days from the date of receipt of the application, the application shall be deemed approved, unless that delay is the result of a reasonable request for additional information." This description concerns the statutory application-processing timeline generally; it does not determine whether any specific application submitted to Maple Grove Homeowners Association concerning 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield was timely processed, denied in writing, delayed by a reasonable request for additional information, or deemed approved under this rule.

RESTRICTIONS AN ASSOCIATION MAY IMPOSE UNDER § 714.1, AND ACTIONS IT MAY NOT TAKE
A separate section of the Solar Rights Act, Civil Code § 714.1, addresses common interest development associations specifically, listing restrictions an association may impose alongside actions it may not take. Section 714.1(a) provides: "Notwithstanding Section 714, an association may impose reasonable provisions that:" restrict solar installations in common areas to association-approved systems, require an owner to obtain association approval before installing a solar energy system in a separate interest owned by someone else, provide for roof and building-component maintenance, repair, or replacement, and require installers to indemnify or reimburse the association or its members for loss or damage the installation, maintenance, or use of the system causes. The statute quotes those four categories as follows: "(1) Restrict the installation of solar energy systems in common areas to those systems approved by the association. (2) Require the owner of a separate interest to obtain the approval of the association for the installation of a solar energy system in a separate interest owned by another. (3) Provide for the maintenance, repair, or replacement of roofs or other building components. (4) Require installers of solar energy systems to indemnify or reimburse the association or its members for loss or damage caused by the installation, maintenance, or use of the solar energy system." Section 714.1(b) then draws a specific line an association may not cross for household rooftop solar: an association "shall not" "[e]stablish a general policy prohibiting the installation or use of a rooftop solar energy system for household purposes on the roof of the building in which the owner resides, or a garage or carport adjacent to the building that has been assigned to the owner for exclusive use," nor "[r]equire approval by a vote of members owning separate interests in the common interest development, including that specified by Section 4600, for installation of a solar energy system for household purposes on the roof of the building in which the owner resides, or a garage or carport adjacent to the building that has been assigned to the owner for exclusive use." The statute makes the consequence explicit: "An action by an association that contravenes paragraph (1) or (2) shall be void and unenforceable." This description concerns the statutory framework generally; it does not determine whether any specific provision, policy, vote requirement, or association action affecting Maple Grove Homeowners Association or 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield complies — or fails to comply — with § 714.1.

REMEDIES FOR A WILLFUL VIOLATION: DAMAGES, CIVIL PENALTY, AND ATTORNEY'S FEES
Civil Code § 714 provides specific remedies tied to noncompliance with the section. Section 714(f) provides: "Any entity, other than a public entity, that willfully violates this section shall be liable to the applicant or other party for actual damages occasioned thereby, and shall pay a civil penalty to the applicant or other party in an amount not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000)." That damages-and-penalty remedy is limited by its own terms to a violation the statute characterizes as "willful" and to a non-public-entity violator. Section 714(g) states a separate, broader fee-shifting rule: "In any action to enforce compliance with this section, the prevailing party shall be awarded reasonable attorney's fees." On its face, § 714(g)'s prevailing-party attorney's-fee rule is not limited to willful violations and is not framed as available only to the applicant; it applies to "any action to enforce compliance with this section." This description concerns the statutory remedies generally; it does not determine whether any specific violation, damages amount, civil penalty, or attorney's-fee award applies to any actual dispute concerning 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield or Maple Grove Homeowners Association.

This clause does not address § 714(h)'s separate public-entity grant-and-loan-eligibility consequence, which applies only to public entities and was not selected for a dedicated clause in this corpus because it does not bear on a private party's rights or remedies.

expectedJSON.body: A separate section of the Solar Rights Act, Civil Code § 714.1, addresses common interest development associations specifically, listing restrictions an association may impose alongside actions it may not take. Section 714.1(a) provides: "Notwithstanding Section 714, an association may impose reasonable provisions that:" restrict solar installations in common areas to association-approved systems, require an owner to obtain association approval before installing a solar energy system in a separate interest owned by someone else, provide for roof and building-component maintenance, repair, or replacement, and require installers to indemnify or reimburse the association or its members for loss or damage the installation, maintenance, or use of the system causes. The statute quotes those four categories as follows: "(1) Restrict the installation of solar energy systems in common areas to those systems approved by the association. (2) Require the owner of a separate interest to obtain the approval of the association for the installation of a solar energy system in a separate interest owned by another. (3) Provide for the maintenance, repair, or replacement of roofs or other building components. (4) Require installers of solar energy systems to indemnify or reimburse the association or its members for loss or damage caused by the installation, maintenance, or use of the solar energy system." The statute makes the consequence explicit: "An action by an association that contravenes paragraph (1) or (2) shall be void and unenforceable."
